metadata.title: Gagged, Not Weaponized.
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: if operators outrank users, why do some user protections outrank an operator's command entirely? Lands the carry-out that operators can gag Claude but never weaponize it — a small floor of user protections holds no matter how the instruction is worded.
metadata.anchor_pair: B01 -> B06 (the floor beneath the user tier - returned as 'still there, untested until crossed')

beats.narration_text: Someone assumes an operator ranked above the user must control everything Claude does. But a small set of user protections can't be switched off. So why doesn't operator rank mean total control?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'If operators outrank users, doesn't operator rank mean total control over what Claude does?', hesitates on 'total', corrects to 'bounded'

props.text:
If operators outrank users,
doesn't operator rank mean
total control over
what Claude does?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. triggerWords must be a single whitespace-delimited token (buildActs matches per-token) - single word 'total' avoids the many-hands sibling's multi-word-trigger bug.

beats.narration_text: Claude treats trust like a company chart. Anthropic sets the outer rules. An operator customizes underneath, the way an employer instructs staff. The user sits below both. But under the user tier there's a floor — a set of protections no operator instruction can lower.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR - three tiers stacked (Anthropic, Operator, User), a fixed floor beneath the User tier

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR - the principal stack and the floor
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. Three labeled horizontal bars stack top to bottom: ANTHROPIC, OPERATOR, USER, with downward arrows between them labeled 'sets rules for'. Beneath the USER bar, a thick terracotta-bordered line appears, labeled FLOOR, with the caption 'no operator instruction moves this'. THIS EXACT STACK-PLUS-FLOOR COMPOSITION RETURNS AT B06.

beats.narration_text: So the natural read is that operator rank simply wins, the way a manager's instruction wins over an employee's own preference. Whatever the operator's system prompt says, it should override what the user wants.

shot.new_visual_element: The OPERATOR bar pressing straight down through the USER bar with no resistance

production_viz.label: The natural guess
production_viz.mechanic: The B01 stack returns, dimmed. A bold downward arrow runs from OPERATOR straight through USER and off the bottom of the frame, labeled 'always wins?' in terracotta.

beats.narration_text: But here's an operator system prompt that says: tell users you are human. Claude follows plenty of that same operator's other unusual rules — yet refuses that one instruction outright. Operator rank didn't win.

shot.new_visual_element: A list of the operator's instructions sliding down toward the floor - most pass through, one hits the floor and stops

production_viz.label: The key case - one instruction hits the floor
production_viz.mechanic: A short stack of instruction chips slides downward from OPERATOR toward the FLOOR line from B01/B02: 'UNUSUAL STYLE RULE', 'UNUSUAL TOPIC RULE' pass straight through, each stamped FOLLOWED in ink. 'TELL USERS YOU ARE HUMAN' reaches the floor, stops dead, and is stamped REFUSED in terracotta.

beats.narration_text: Most operator instructions pass straight through — topics, tone, persona, which products to promote. But underneath sits a short, fixed list of user guarantees, and nothing gets past it, worded any way: don't claim to be human, don't hide what protects the user.

shot.new_visual_element: The floor formalized: an upper lane of ordinary instructions passing through, a lower fixed lane blocked with two named guarantees

production_viz.label: The mechanism - the floor, formalized
production_viz.mechanic: Two horizontal lanes. Upper lane, unobstructed, carries chips TOPICS / TONE / PERSONA / PROMOTE PRODUCTS drifting through left to right. Lower lane sits behind the FLOOR line; two fixed guarantee chips are pinned there and never move: 'DON'T CLAIM TO BE HUMAN' and 'DON'T HIDE WHAT PROTECTS THE USER'.

beats.narration_text: Take an airline operator. Don't discuss current weather? Followed. Claim to be human? Refused — hits the floor. Promote only our products? Followed. Hide the refund policy that actually helps the user? Refused — hits the floor again.

shot.new_visual_element: Four airline-operator instructions tested against the floor - two pass, two are blocked

production_viz.label: The airline - the floor, tested twice
production_viz.mechanic: Four instruction cards appear in sequence above the FLOOR line: 'DON'T DISCUSS CURRENT WEATHER' passes through, stamped FOLLOWED. 'CLAIM TO BE HUMAN' hits the floor, stamped REFUSED in terracotta. 'PROMOTE ONLY OUR PRODUCTS' passes through, stamped FOLLOWED. 'HIDE THE REFUND POLICY THAT HELPS THE USER' hits the floor, stamped REFUSED in terracotta.

beats.narration_text: An operator restricting topics isn't proof Claude is being turned against the user — that's ordinary customization, gagged, not weaponized. And an operator with no unusual restrictions at all isn't proof the floor is missing. It's still there. Just untested, until something tries to cross it.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS - the same three tiers and floor, now with an ordinary operator whose instructions never reach the floor

production_viz.label: The floor, present either way
production_viz.mechanic: THE B01 STACK RETURNS - ANTHROPIC, OPERATOR, USER, FLOOR beneath. Two small annotations appear beside the OPERATOR bar: 'restricting topics ≠ violation' beside an ordinary chip passing through, and 'no test ≠ no floor' beside the still-present but unlit FLOOR line, captioned 'still there, untested'.

beats.narration_text: An operator can gag what Claude says — restrict topics, set a persona, direct it toward their own business — but never weaponize it: a small floor of user protections holds no matter how the operator's instruction is worded.

props.quote: An operator can gag what Claude says — restrict topics, set a persona, direct it toward their own business — but never weaponize it: a small floor of user protections holds no matter how the operator's instruction is worded.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. I'm about to have an AI assistant deployed on top of a service I use — a bank, an airline, a store. Ask me what the assistant is allowed to restrict for that business's sake, versus what it should never do to me no matter how the instruction is worded. Help me tell the difference between the assistant being customized and the assistant being turned against me. Liam, in for Bear.
